definition: An arcing (multi-axis) motion path stays visually readable across a wider range of viewing angles than a linear, single-axis motion, because a straight-line move toward or away from the camera can collapse to near-zero apparent screen-space movement from some angles, while an arc always has motion on more than one axis.
purpose: Keep an action readable when the camera angle is not authored or fixed in advance — a game with a player-controlled camera cannot guarantee any one viewing angle, unlike film.
visible_effect: A wide swipe or sweep reads clearly as motion from nearly any camera angle; a direct forward stab or thrust can look like almost nothing is happening when viewed close to head-on, because most of its motion is compressed into the depth axis the camera itself is looking down.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: A player who cannot read an attack's motion from their current camera angle loses the readability benefit that action was supposed to provide, independent of how well-animated it is from the "intended" angle — which, in an interactive context, does not exist.
physical_interpretation: Purely a projection/viewing-geometry fact, not a claim about the physical motion itself: the SAME arc is equally "real" from every angle, but its on-SCREEN legibility is not, because screen-space motion is the 2D projection of a 3D path.
use_cases: any action in a 3D game with a player-controlled (not fixed/authored) camera
an attack, ability, or telegraph specifically meant to be read by the player regardless of their current camera framing
choosing a swipe/sweep over a direct thrust when both would otherwise communicate the same intent
non_use_cases: a fixed-camera or cutscene context (film, a scripted in-engine cinematic) where the camera angle IS known in advance and arcs can be tuned to that one specific view instead
an action deliberately meant to be hard to read (rare, but the same logic in reverse applies to a "hidden tell" design)
a purely first-person action where the acting part has no external viewing angle to be robust against in the first place
interactions: Arcs — this is a game-specific reason to prefer arcs over the existing card's general "organic and appealing" reasoning; it applies even to a mechanical or stylized character where the classical appeal argument would not

Staging — Part 26.3's own list of open questions already names "is the action readable in the active camera" as something this build cannot check for lack of a camera model; this entry sharpens WHY that check matters specifically for arcs
Startup frame budget — a fast, hard-to-read arc and a fast, hard-to-read stab fail for compounding reasons if both are also short on startup frames

style_variations.game_combat: the primary context this reasoning applies to; the more free the player camera, the more this consideration matters
style_variations.cinematic: the constraint that motivates this entry (an unknown camera angle) does not apply, so a director may deliberately choose an axial, camera-forward motion for a specific authored shot

cadence_representation: Not represented, and not straightforwardly checkable: `ai/motion.js MOT-005` measures path curvature and chord deviation in WORLD space, which is exactly the data needed, but judging whether that path stays legible across a RANGE of camera angles requires a camera/viewing model this build does not have — the same honestly-stated gap the existing `staging` and `arcs` entries already name for camera-dependent questions generally.
control_surface: `analyze_motion` reports world-space curvature; nothing projects that curvature through a range of hypothetical camera angles to judge multi-angle readability.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Partially buildable: given curvature/chord-deviation data already measured per MOT-005, and a declared set of candidate camera angles, screen-space apparent motion at each angle is a projection computation this build could in principle run — but no code does, since Cadence has no active-camera model at all (the same limitation named throughout this table for anything camera-dependent).
failure_modes: choosing a linear/axial motion for an action that needs to read from an unknown player camera angle, discovering only in playtesting (from specific angles) that it reads as barely moving
over-applying this and making every action a wide swipe regardless of what the action actually is, which is its own readability and believability problem
roblox_considerations: Directly relevant: Roblox's default camera is player-controlled in the overwhelming majority of experiences, so this consideration applies by default rather than as an edge case.
examples: a wide sword swipe reading clearly from nearly any angle, versus a direct forward spear/thrust that can look like almost no motion at all from a near-head-on camera angle — both shown side by side in the source footage (video 6 @ 4:19–4:39, a direct-thrust stance confirmed on screen at t=4:27–4:31 alongside a wide-swipe attack at t=4:35–4:52)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/lOzgxMgAnxQ @ 4:19–4:39 — Dan states the swipe-vs-stab reasoning directly, illustrated with matching gameplay footage of both attack types; experimental until validated
